title: Tabletop Battles Reviews: Blood Bowl Spike! Magazine (Sevens Rules) and Pitch 2026
content:
Well hi-de-hi sports ball fans! Welcome to the Tabletop Battles review of Spike 22 aka the Blood Bowl Sevens edition! Spike! Magazine is BACK with issue 22 and this one is ALL about the popular ‘Sevens’ format of Blood Bowl. There is also a new pitch to go with and we have had a good nose of that too! As always our thanks go out to Games Workshop for providing us with an early copy for us to sink-gnaw our abnormally large in both size and number of teeth into!

Spike! Issue 22.
Games Workshop

Games Workshop are also releasing THREE new plastic big guys today, go HERE for all our thoughts on these BIG new additions to your Blood Bowl roster.

Why Play Sevens Blood Bowl?

Spike! Issue 22. Credit: Games Workshop

Badusernametag: Blood Bowl Sevens is a smaller, faster-paced game than regular Elevens, which presents coaches with differing challenges and play styles while maintaining all the carnage and mayhem that you'll have come to expect from a full match. The fluff is that Sevens games are the amateur and semi-pro leagues underneath the majors, with players coming up and trying to make it BIG in the beautiful, bloody game.

Dakari-Mane: It's a great way to get your Blood Bowl fix in if you need to play at lunch or if you want to get more games in than you'd otherwise be able to in a day. It’s shorter in turns and is played on a smaller pitch, so you get a truncated experience, but with the full rules. A big core difference here is that the two teams' lines of scrimmage are further apart, so you don’t get to throw blocks at each other right from the off. This means it can be a cagier game, with more ball play, ducking, diving and dodging!

The Fluff

Dakari-Mane: As always, there's some amazing background included in this edition of Spike! covering where Sevens originated, how it spread, and the ongoing popularity of the game in the Old World; there's also "Dirt from the Dugout", "Chat with the Rat", "Ask Lord Borak" and "Coffin Corner," which add some lighthearted fun.

Badusernametag: I’d not paid Spike(!) much attention before and it’s a really nicely formatted piece of work. Engaging from the beginning for a fan and a player. The layout, production and art are spot on, rules presentation aside. The in-world adverts are pretty hilarious:

Amazing art on these in game ads!! Spike! Issue 22. Credit: Games Workshop

The Rules

Badusernametag: There's a lot going on here and this is a definite expansion of the Sevens rules presented in Deathzone last season. We will mainly focus on changes here, as most of this has been covered before. We assume you have a basic idea of the OG Sevens rules.

Team Building

Previously you could take any number of your large volume linos (the 0-12 or 0-16 options) and up to four other players. Now you can only have any number of Lineman Keyword players and then four other players. This has a big impact for teams with multiple types of Lineman on the roster. This is a very big buff to Old World Alliance, who have a variety of useful linemen. The changes are also very useful for Humans & Orcs, both of which have cheap stunty lineman access. You might not have had space on the squad for a goblin, but if they’re just replacing a Lino and not a Blitzter they might just make the squad!!

Chaos Renegades and Underworld Denizens LOVE this. Chaos Renegades open up all their fun and flavourful types of Lineman and can still take a thrower and big guys. Whilst Skaven can now take as many Snots and Grots as they like! Both teams are also functionally unaffected by these rules as each team only has 4 non-lineman players available on their roster!? (Well kinda Dakari-Mane, they can still only take four non-linemen, they just could have one of each!!!). Chaos Dwarves suffer somewhat from not having the Lineman keyword.

Whereas Snotlings seem to get scuppered, as the Insignificant trait doesn't allow them to include more players with insignificant than those without & they're restricted to four non-insignificant players. So I guess you're running two Trolls, two Pump Wagons & four Snotlings!

Re-rolls flat 100,000 GP from double. Definitely a change I'm in favour of as for many teams forking out over 100k made a RR unaffordable. Cheerleaders are 0-6 now, No big thing. Dedicated as fans restricted to +1 at time of drafting. This makes sense for ‘Rookie’ teams. Veteran - 1 player per team -1ma, but gains "semi-pro" (1 per game RR for pick up, pass, catch or self inflicted pow in a block) a useful little addition to the team,  particularly when re-rolls are 100k.

Team Creation

CrabStuffedMushrooms: The change in Lineman definition to the Keyword instead of the 0-12/0-16 restrictions is clean and easier to understand, but it has some interesting effects. Namely, I think it makes OWA and UW incredibly flexible - and they are already amazing teams. It lets OWA in particular put a lot of skills on the pitch. I made a few 600gp teams, and they were certainly great. But I think with cash, the teams could grow into real monsters if they can get an extra Dwarf or Linerat.

I think overall, the flexibility this affords to allow things like Halflings on the field is worth it. It is clean and easy to understand. They didn’t seem to accommodate the Insignificant trait, which is an easy fix, but creates a problem in the moment.

Loner 5+ change for Journeymen is really fun, and while I don’t think it will have a big impact with how rarely rerolls are used, I bet it happens in clutch moments from time to time in a way that hilariously ruins a drive.

I like the flat 100k reroll. The former method of doubling the cost was extra punishing for some of the more expensive team rerolls. I think this is just cheap enough that some people may opt for the Team reroll at creation, and hope to fill in their positionals with more cash as a league progresses. Veteran player rule is amazing fluff, is unevenly impactful from team to team, and I love it.

Inducements

Like 11s, the big thing here is that Prayers to Nuffle are too impactful. Especially since you can use your own Treasury on them, it seems hard not to take them. Rerolling duplicates means you are almost guaranteed at least one really good result.

  • The Desperate Measures retool is great and keeps the energy of the original. 
  • Sports Espionage was already insane, and now TWO rerolls is pretty crazy.
  • Set Piece still adds some dice rolls instead of being automatic. It prevents an auto-score situation.
  • Discarded Banana Skin is going to be easy to forget, but it creates a tension similar to Magic Scroll where you have to think about it the whole game!
  • Unfortunately, Prayers to Nuffle dilute the desperate measures a little. I think it will front-load too many random rolls at the start of the match. A TV difference of 5k to 10k does not need balancing.
  • I wish Team Mascot was available for 50k.

In Game

Dakari-Mane: The Kick off table has had a thorough going over like a fallen Dragon Prince surrounded by goblins. Many entries have been tightened up with minor tweaks, amendments or changes.

2 - Get the Ref: No change.

3 - Time Out: Turn 5+ now instead of turn 4+.

4 - Alert Defense: May move into no man's land.

5 - High Kick: May move into no man's land.

6 - Cheering Fans: Block assist.

7 - Brilliant Coaching: No change.

8 - Changing Weather: No change.

9 - Quick Snap: No change.

10 - CHARGE!: D3+1 open teammates can move. Alternatively: one can blitz, one can throw a teammate, and one can kick a teammate instead.

11 - Dodgy Snack: Roll off, loser selects a random player 2+ -1ma, av for drive, on a 1 off for the drive.

12 - Pitch Invasion: Only 1 player now.

Amateur referee: Reflecting the less prestigious nature of Sevens, the quality of the referees cannot be guaranteed - argue the call succeeds on a 5+.

Throw-in distance is now d6+2 and kick of scatter is now "roll 2d6, pick the lowest." This is a nice change that reduces scatter to reflect the smaller size of the Sevens pitch. Fewer wild throws and kicks that always go off the pitch!

Badusernametag: One of my (few) gripes with the first version of Sevens was the ambiguity over how you resolved kick offs. The Deathzone rules told you to kick off as normal, but not having a single central Line of Scrimmage didn’t allow for that to be resolved clearly. You place the ball in “your opponents half”, but does that include no mans land? When is a Touchback triggered? I was hoping this would be resolved in the new rules and it’s not really.

So it doesn’t define where you place the ball. So we assume your opponents “half” is half way through no mans land again, although it does tell you its not a touchback if the ball goes into no mans land. So an improvement at least!?

League Play

Dakari-Mane: A whole section dedicated to the best way to play the beautiful game!
  • Journeymen: Due to this being the rookie leagues, a Journeyman that joins your team to get you up to 7 players has the loner (5+) trait. Probably best off avoiding doing anything with them then!
  • Desperate Measures: The table has been updated from last edition & you can take up to five of them.
  • Prayers to Nuffle: A modified table is included & teams can have up to 2 rolls.
  • Player Advancement: no player may gain leader or pro.

Nobility comes in clutch here with a potential four pros in the starting line-up! I'm unclear as to how this rule interacts with the team captain rule; do you only gain the 6+ re-roll retention? Probably needs clarification.

Skill Progression 

After each game you can either:

  • Randomly generate a primary skill from a stack of three (you choose two, your opponent chooses one) by rolling a d3 for a player of your choice
  • Randomly give a secondary skill to a random player.

Players leaving the team after gaining skills remains the same as last edition, however they have added an option to pay a player to stay, at the reasonable price of what they cost (base player cost plus skills), however if you pay a player to stay,  their cost increases, meaning they'll cost more to keep on the team the next time someone tries to poach them!

I can really see this driving people towards not skilling up particularly expensive players. Would you risk your wardancer quitting the team after ever game?

CrabStuffedMushrooms: I think the new advancement randomization is a great balance between control and chaos. Almost all trees have several great skills to choose from. It will be fun to see the vibe between player groups for your opponent to also pick a good skill or to mess with you. I wish there was still an Elite skill tax of some kind. If it was totally random, I would understand. But since you get to pick your stabs at Dodge, Block, etc., some sort of premium would still be warranted. They are just too good and get even better with lack of rerolls.

In the previous version, any player on the team could advance. Now, players have to not be taken out as a casualty. This will add more excitement to losing a player to a casualty, as Lasting Injuries don’t happen, and Death is almost as rare as in 11s. I like that you can pay to maintain your drafted player, but I don’t like that your advanced player may get taken before you even get to play a single game with them. 

Because the Drafting Players step happens before the Hiring, Firing, and Temporarily Retiring step, you will get to buy a replacement player before the next game. So this is a bit of a salve, but still requires you to have cash. Love the ban of Leader and Pro for chosen skills, but like that it could still randomly pop up if anyone was crazy enough to do a Secondary Skill.

The new hiring restrictions continue to be a thing I think is fluffy and fun, but may be even more punishing for leagues in sevens. There are no lasting injuries, but we may go into key games down a couple of positionals for Serious Injuries, which is a big deal if you only have four!

New Rules

Dakari-Mane: There are modified rules for redrafting Sevens teams for new seasons, and a matched play section describing how to run tournaments of Sevens, covering drafting a team, inducements, star player points, team tiers & skills. Most interesting to me is that there will be a revised tier list being released to reflect how different teams perform under the Sevens rules.

Then we have five example Sevens teams -- Skaven, Norse, Goblin, Khorne & Chaos Chosen. Each team listing comes with a "how to play this team" guide and a "what to do when you start skilling up" guide.

Badusernametag: We really like this as a concept. Fun, thematic, mixes hobby with rules and makes a nice package of it all as a team building display. Would like it if they did more of them. Maybe in a future release? This is the kind of copy that really makes this release interesting as well as just being rules content. 

New Sevens Pitch 2026

Badusernametag: The new pitch comes in the exact same size as the original and comes with the same two small format dugouts as well. The design here is generic, simply bringing the Sevens pitch up to date in design with the third season pitch and dugouts. It’s neat and looks good.

I like that the endzones are distinct and clear colours in this new one.

Bloodbowl Sevens Pitch 2026 Credit: crabbedstuffmushrooms

Bloodbowl Sevens Pitch 2026. Credit: crabbedstuffmushrooms

Final Thoughts

Dakari-Mane: Overall we’re in favour of the tweaks and changes that have been made, it's tightened things up nicely and reined in some of the potentially apocalyptic kick-off table results. The matched play rules look like a great way to play one off pick-up games where you can each have some upgrades. I'm genuinely looking forward to playing some sevens again. And once the official Sevens team tier list drops, I might even give running a one -ay event a go.

Badusernametag: Sevens continues apace as the fast and furious way to crack out a game of Blood Bowl. Really pleased to see it grow a new lease of life in these comprehensive and dedicated rules for the third season. It will continue to be my favourite way for a friendly or a teaching game, but with these new and developed rules for leagues and tourneys it may gain a greater life yet. Seven is my new lucky number.

Until next time, happy gnawing on the bones of your enemies!

Spike! Issue 22. Credit: Games Workshop Have any questions or feedback? Drop us a note in the comments below or email us at contact@tabletopbattles.com. Want articles like this linked in your inbox every Monday morning? Sign up for our newsletter. And don't forget that you can support us on Patreon for backer rewards like early video content, Administratum access, an ad-free experience on our website, and subscriber-only content covering competitive Warhammer 40K!

title: Tabletop Battles Reviews: Blood Bowl Big Guys 2026
content:
Hey hey sports fans! Tabletop Battles are reporting today on everyone’s favourite gruesome sport, Blood Bowl! Games Workshop are releasing a throng of three thicc plastic big guys alongside the new Spike! Journal mag and Sevens pitch. Games Workshop were nice enough to send us all of these to review, so we’ve been taking a time out to have fun with muscle and analyse the new rules for Sevens. Let's see what's happening.

What's being released?

  • Morg ‘n’ Thorg (Star player, available to any non-Undead team)
  • Rat Ogre (plays for Chaos Renegades, Skaven, Underworld Denizens)
  • Minotaur (plays for Chaos Chosen, Chaos Dwarves, Chaos Renegades)
  • New Blood Bowl Sevens pitch (and dugouts)
  • Spike! Journal issue 22 (Rules periodical, focusing on new Sevens rules)

For the Rules and Pitch review go HERE.

Morg ‘n Thorg - Star Ogre Blitzer

Morg ’n’ Thorg 2026. Credit: Games Workshop

Multi-part plastic kit- reimagining of the best known Star Player in Blood Bowl history.

Bloodbowl 3rd edition box art 1994. Credit: Games Workshop

Badusernametag: Morg ‘n’ Thorg is THE classic Star Player of the Blood Bowl Mini-verse. Alongside original stars like Griff Oberwald he has been smashing jaws on the Gridiron for 30+ years and is still going strong. He was on the cover of the original game and then again on the cover of the 3rd ed boxed set that came out in 1994. That box art is SUCH an iconic piece of Blood Bowl imagery. Always stuck with me and as a child I was really inspired by it. GW often seem to be selling nostalgia nowadays and I’m sometimes unsure, but this one is great work and I’m here for it. They’ve reimagined the OG Morg ‘n’ Thorg pose that I loved as a kid, bashing hand over head and fist in front. This lump of lead went on a 40mm square base back when there was nothing else but 25mm rounds! It’s thoughtfully done (ironic much) and has long time Blood Bowl fans firmly in mind!

OG Morg ’n’ thorg Metal model. Credit: Warhammer Community

The previous Morg sized-up with the latest model. Credit: CrabStuffedMushrooms

This new rendition of Morg is bigger and meaner than ever; he comes with options that are in turn broadly Orc themed, Chaos themed and Imperial themed. The background is that the various options relate to the stages of his career; he starts playing for the Chaos Allstars, does a stint in the badlands with the Orcs, and then ends up with the Imperial Reikland Reivers. It’s a well constructed story for the options in the box and has the narrative in mind. Honestly, there is no reason not to mix and match the bits and build the best Morg for you!

Morg ’n’ Thorg Sprue- bursting with bits!

Morg ’N’ Thorg 2026- Ogre Star Blitzer.
Credit: @badusernametag

I went with the Bald head and Orc coded stuff, as it just appealed to me more. The touches are nice; the necklace of fetishes collected from across his career, the gawdy rings, the old school mohawk on the ‘chaos’ head. This would make a great alternative for a Blood Bowl Ogre for any team if you don’t see yourself using a $300k+ Star Player that often, especially for a Badlands or Chaos team, as the regular plastic model is more Imperial Themed. It’s a much more dynamic model than the regular Blood Bowl Ogre.

Took a moment out of painting Ogors to paint a new and exciting Ogre instead! I’ve painted mine in a random colour scheme that has nothing to do with any of my teams, went for flashy blue and yellow, as Morg is a BIG star and needs some bling.

If I were starting a Renegades or Nobility team soon, I’d deffo grab Morg just to add a really badass Ogre to my team.

Morg ’N’ Thorg 2026- Ogre Star Blitzer.
Credit: @badusernametag

Morg ’N’ Thorg 2026- Ogre Star Blitzer. Credit: @badusernametag

Blood Bowl Minotaur

Spike! Issue 22. Credit: Games Workshop Liam: The Minotaur is a classic Big Guy for Chaos, and here comes one in plastic. It’s a neat kit, with two basic builds - a generic Chaos Minotaur, and then a specific one for Chaos Dwarfs with the particular stylings for that team, mostly in the form of an appropriately big hat. It’s not that big on a Minotaur’s head of course, but it’s the thought that counts.

Your other choices represent possible upgrades to the Minotaur - a normal or mutated tail, and normal or mutated fists/claws. I went with mostly stock choices here, though I preferred the mutated tail aesthetically if nothing else.

The build on this guy is pretty straightforward, and he’s lovely to paint - it’s a very open pose, and in the Chaos Dwarf version at least there’s lots of nice open surfaces with hard edges for a classic GW base and highlight approach. There’s enough detail to make him look good, but he’s not at all busy. I painted him in a couple of sessions and enjoyed it the whole time.

Chaos Dwarfs Minotaur. Credit: Corrode

Rat Ogre

Spike! Issue 22. Credit: Games Workshop

Dakari-Mane: As a life long Blood Bowl fan, big guys are, to me, very much at the heart of the game. The wonderful image by Brett Ewins from the first edition box of Morg'n'Thorg smashing his way through an assortment of players with a goblin stuffed under his arm is one of my foundational memories of the game. 

If a team has a big guy, then when I play that team it WILL have a big guy on the board.

The Rat Ogre is to my mind an amazing player on the pitch. As fast as a Kroxigor and as agile as an Ogre, which is technically neither that fast nor that agile, but compared to the other big guys it's dancing with the best. They make an amazing back-stop/sweeper and if you give them break tackle & two heads they dodge on a 0+, and so could walk into a 3 tackle zone cage on a 3+! Love em! 

Assembly

This big cheese stealing boi went together without any major issues, the only bit that was at all fiddly being the initial main torso assembly; once that was done everything else slotted together nicely. Also he's got LOADS of options. Three heads (would have been nice to have had an option to fit two of them at once maybe?), an alternative left arm with claws, two tails, two loincloths and most importantly a choice of three shoulder spikes, two of which have tiny ride along rat-buddies on them that are doing stuff. 

I went with the armoured head & loincloth, non-mutated arm, weaponised mace tail & the rat with the cheese & flag. 

MawQueenMinis: The kit went together great, but there were less options than expected. The box makes it seem like there are shoulder pad options - but it's just different paint schemes. The little rat on the shoulder is such a cute touch!

Paint Guide

Dakari-Mane:

Sprayed it grey, wet/dry brushed the whole mini in white (Minimalist Zenithal). The advantage of the bigger Skaven gribblies is that once you've done the flesh you're 75% of the way there, so that's where we'll start. 

  • Guilliman flesh all over the flesh. 
  • Carroburg crimson into all the shadows, recesses & wherever I wanted a bit more ruddy flesh colour. 
  • Ratling grime for the fur. 
  • Came back in with kislev flesh (thinned with lahmian medium) as a highlight. 

It's Blood Bowl, so team colours ought to be as garish & clashing as possible. The Hellpit Cheese Stealers wear orange and green, so it's Magmadroth Flame & Striking Scorpion Green. A tiny dot of Flash Gitz Yellow went to each as a highlight; once dry, a wash was applied, Biel Tan Green & Gryph-hound Orange (diluted with Lahmian Medium) to the appropriate colours. 

Horns, spikes, claws & teeth were all painted in Skeleton Horde, then highlighted with Skeleton Horde and White Scar up till nearly pure White Scar. 

Rhinox Hide was sponged over anything I wanted to make look worn or damaged. 

Iron Hands sSeel picked out all the metal details and was used to spot in the centre of the Rhinox Hide damaged areas. 

Next I wanted to tie things together so I went in with Agrax Earthshade round the eyes, over the metal, in the deeper shadows & across the bones/horns/teeth & claws. 

The finishing details: Pustules were a spot of Yriel Yellow & a wash of Carroburg Crimson so they look sore. 

The cheese the rat is holding was picked out in Nazdreg Yellow.

And the steel bits were given a patchy Gryph-hound Orange wash to represent rust. 

The base was sand textured before priming, painted Steel Legion Drab & highlighted with Zandri Dust. 

At this point all it needs is varnishing & some tufts adding. 

An important thing to remember when applying a matt spray varnish is that you should be careful of temperature and humidity as excess of either can cause the matt varnish to dry in the air which causes a terrible paint job ruining misting or fogging to occur. Ask me how I know!

When matt varnish goes awry!
Credit: @dakarimane

After you have repainted your miniature & hand painted on your matt varnish you can apply your tufts to the base and call it done.

Lovely miniature, well worthy addition to the team, a pleasure to paint (twice!).

Bloodbowl Rat Ogre 2026. Credit: @Dakarimane (insta)

Bloodbowl Rat Ogre 2026. Credit: @Dakarimane (insta)

Bloodbowl Rat Ogre 2026. Credit: @Dakarimane (insta)

Final Thoughts

Three big new additions to the beautiful game. Whilst Bloodbowl has many wonderful sculpts in resin from ForgeWorld, it really helps to get an injection of Big Guys in basic plastic. These are more affordable and accessible, allow for more conversion opportunities and just fill out the range. With these three models you can now have a Chaos Renegades team with only GW core models and without touching resin!! 

Three great sculpts, including the most (in)famous player of all time. This is a great release and we’re here for it.

title: Tabletop Battles Reviews: Warhammer The Old World - Lord on Chaos Dragon
content:
Hot on the heels of the new Warriors of Chaos characters, Knights and Warriors, heavy reinforcement arrives in the form of the Lord on Chaos Dragon, which Rich has gotten his hands on. Our thanks to Games Workshop for providing an advanced copy of this kit.

Lord on Chaos Dragon. Credit: Warhammer Community

What’s In the Box?

Screaming out of hellspawned clouds in a dazzling display of fury, the new Lord on Chaos Dragon has reached the shores of the Old World and is ready to rain fire down on any man, dwarf or elf unfortunate enough to get in its way. Alternatively, your Chaos horde can be reinforced by a powerful Sorcerer on Chaos Dragon, slinging spells from atop their deadly steed. Whichever option is chosen, the kit comes with spare legs and a base to build the alternate rider as a foot hero instead, making sure as much of the kit as possible is used.

Chaos Lord on Dragon sprues. Credit: Rich Nutter

The chunky box is filled with a hefty array of sprues, plus a 30mm square base for the foot character and a 100x150mm base for the dragon itself. A lot of the parts on these sprues are quite three-dimensional, sticking out above or below the main plane of the sprue, and on my kit a couple of pieces had detached themselves from the frames whilst in the box, presumably due to impact. They were present and correct, rattling around the bottom of the box, but just a warning to check before cracking on with the build.

Assembly

Large models for The Old World have been a bit of a mixed bag. Although the sculpts have been excellent, there have been instances such as the Cathay Sentinel, or my experience with Miao Ying, where it felt like either the kit engineering or the instruction steps are letting down the build experience a little. It’s pleasing to be able to say, then, that there’s very little of that in the Chaos Dragon kit. The dragon goes together step by step, with subassemblies that make sense, and I didn’t encounter a single bit of “hold these two parts by a tiny connection while you thread something in between them”.

Chaos Lord on Dragon, built. Credit: Rich Nutter

Overall that made the build experience a lot more fun, and I powered through the kit in a couple of hours. We just got a nice new Chaos Lord on foot from the Core Set, and the Sorcerer packed in with the Battle March box is a comparatively old sculpt, so I decided on the combo of a nice new Sorcerer on foot sculpt plus a big combat Lord who could go and get stuck in. The Sorcerer is stuck with their staff, but the lord has a choice of a sword or halberd/lance in one hand, and a shield or axe in the other. I went for the giant sword option. The dragon has a little bit of customisation in its heads - each upper head can go on either neck, and the horns are interchangeable, but otherwise its pose is locked.

Two heads, Jeremy? Credit: Rich Nutter

As I was building the model it started to become clear that it was going to end up rather large, and once finished, it’s absolutely huge. The dragon stands 275mm (nearly 11”) from base to wingtip, and 300mm (almost 12”) across from wingtip to wingtip. That’s a hair off as tall as the Archaon model from Age of Sigmar (the current standard for “big dragon”), and wider to boot. This is the large centrepiece that the Warriors of Chaos army list has been waiting for, in my opinion - it makes the Sorcerer on Manticore look tiny by comparison.

Chaos Sorcerer on foot. Credit: Rich Nutter

Of final note for the building process, the rider, throne and dragon can all be built completely separately. This was useful for painting in subassemblies, but also lets you build a riderless dragon if you so prefer. It leaves a small divot in the top scales where a chain would attach, but it’s not really noticeable and could be easily puttied if you really wanted to cover it.

The rider and saddle are easily sub-assemblied. Credit: Rich Nutter

Warhammer Community have made much of the ability to build the riderless variant of the dragon, even suggesting that it could be a stand-in for Galrauch the Great Drake. Whilst this would be a hell of a glow up, and seems intentional given the two-headed nature of this beast, it’s worth noting that at the time of publishing Galrauch’s profile is on a 60x100mm base, which this dragon would not fit on. On the off chance it could be made to fit, it would probably fall over. It doesn’t seem like the Arcane Journal features an update to Galrauch’s profile, or a new profile for a Chaos Dragon without rider, so although it’s possible that this comes in an FAQ (other profiles have been updated to have a varied range of base sizes in the past), my advice for now is to not assume that this is a stealth Galrauch update.

Painting

As is often the case with these reviews, I was left with less time to paint the Lord on Chaos Dragon than the average hobbyist, so I was left thinking up ways to minimise my brush time whilst still having a good tabletop impact. I knew that I wanted the characters to match the Warrior I’d already painted, grimy and weathered, and so that wouldn’t take too much time, but I was really keen to make the dragon itself pop.

Chaos Lord on Drago, with some volumetric highlighting I definitely didn’t forget to take this until after I’d started the green, honest. Credit: Rich Nutter

I started off by priming the pieces in Colour Forge Raven Black Spray, before airbrushing some very broad volumetric highlights onto the dragon’s musculature and wings using a thinned white paint. Most of the model was then sprayed with 2-3 thin coats of Warhammer Colour Contrast Aeldari Emerald to achieve a rich green colour, with harder, scaled areas followed up by a brushed-on coat of Warhammer Colour Contrast Black Templar. Where possible, I feathered the edges of the Black Templar coat to ease the transition between green and black areas.

After this it was time for the time-saver’s best friend: drybrushing. Green areas were given an all over drybrush of Mini Colour Verdigris (NB: This is a prototype bottle left over from our review, and at time of writing Mini Colour is yet to hit shelves - I suggest Warhammer Colour Sybarite Green as a substitute). Black areas were drybrushed heavily with Two Thin Coats Death Reaper to smooth out the contrast coat, before a final drybrush of Two Thin Coats Shadow Blue.

Chaos Lord on Dragon, now green. Credit: Rich Nutter

I decided on red wing membranes and horns/spikes to add some colour contrast to the model to make it pop, which is a good speed painting tip if you’re looking for high impact in a short amount of time. These were based in Warhammer Colour Khorne Red, and then drybrushed with Warhammer Colour Evil Sunz Scarlet and Warhammer Colour Wild Rider Red. In an ideal world I think I would have spent a bit more time on this step and started from Evil Sunz Scarlet and gone up to orange highlights to make the whole thing brighter, but I was on a timescale and very reliant on the intense coverage of Khorne Red to save me some time! The eyes were dotted in with Warhammer Colour Phalanx Yellow.

As a final step on the dragon, I mixed some Warhammer Colour Agrax Earthshade, Nuln Oil and Lahmian Medium in a 1:1:1 ratio, and slathered it all over the model, making sure to try and avoid pooling/running where possible. I didn’t succeed fully, but my Warriors of Chaos are quite grimy anyway so it’s no huge issue. This darklines the model, helping to up the contrast a little, and also helps to bring it back to the grimy vibes of the armoured warriors and make them seem like they exist in the same universe.

Chaos Lord on Dragon. Credit: Rich Nutter

The Lord and Sorcerer were based in a variety of dark metals, browns, and flesh tones, before being washed with Agrax Earthshade and then weathered with rust and verdigris (mostly Warhammer Colour blues, greens, browns and oranges). Warhammer Colour technical paints like Blood for the Blood God help to further grime them up. For the Lord’s magical weapons, I based the blades in Warhammer Colour Contrast Imperial Fist, smoothed out with Phalanx Yellow. I then drybrushed/stippled up through oranges, reds and blacks to give the forged metal look.

Chaos Lord on Dragon. Credit: Rich Nutter

As a final step, bases got an all over coat of KrautCover Tale of Grimdark basing mix (yes, the one with the bones), locked in place with PVA and isopropyl alcohol. Finally, everything was varnished with a couple of coats of Two Thin Coats Satin Varnish, thinned 1:1 through the airbrush. And with that, the Lord on Chaos Dragon, and accompanying Sorcerer, are complete!

Chaos Sorcerer. Credit: Rich Nutter

Wrap Up

What a kit! Is this the best miniature released for The Old World so far? It’s certainly one of the largest and most impactful, and it’s great to see Warriors of Chaos getting updated and diverging slightly from the Slaves to Darkness Age of Sigmar incarnation. This kit is bound to turn heads on the table, and I’m looking forward to continuing to build a Chaos army around it.

title: Gencon 2026 Infinity Seminar - The Tabletop Battles Hot Take
content:
As is their custom, Corvus Belli have held a preview seminar at GenCon where they showed off some upcoming stuff for Warcrow, Hexadome Tactics, and Infinity. It's the latter which is our special interest, so we're going to talk about some of the main points. If you would like to watch the seminar video in full, it's available here.

Changes to Aerial Vehicles Incoming

In a very welcome acknowledgement of a major issue affecting competitive events, CB have said they will be taking some kind of action to rein in Vehicles. There's no indication at all what that might be yet.

  • Musterkrux: I really just want to see a light touch from CB here. It'll only take a nudge here and there for Flyers to be balanced appropriately. Too much and they'll become entirely non-viable. Also, while there is data to be collected in listening to your community and taking measured action, turning Infinity into a game where Round Zero is whinging hard enough that the company nerfs your opponent's faction harder than yours gets nerfed is a mistake the war-gaming community has already made at least once before (Warmachine's Community Integrated Development, if you're wondering).
  • Genghis: I'm not too worried about that. CB have made it clear that they do gather data wherever possible, looking at factions' win rates and the inclusion of different profiles within tournament army lists. That isn't to say collecting that data is without challenges, but they do try. I'm more interested to see whether they go purely with a points-based solution, or walk back some of Vehicles' unique strengths. I personally think the upper limits of their current mobility need to be examined. 11" of true flight movement in a single Order while firing, combined with the advantages of Silhouette 7 size when vaulting terrain, is just too hard to balance against conventional units.

Forthcoming Releases

One of September's releases, this lovely new Gecko TAG for Nomads/Corregidor will be in Unicool, like all their new bigger models, and interestingly it's the first Nomad TAG to be packaged with the Robbybot Peripheral Ancillary.

  • Genghis: I'm in the awkward position of being someone who never really runs more than 1 Gecko in a list, and has a painted metal one I'm happy with. But this sculpt is a real step up and I am certainly planning to pick one up.
  • Musterkrux: I like it, though I think those massive shoulder-pads are selling it as a much bigger, meaner TAG than it actually is. It's a very cool sculpt and all the other factions should be jealous that Nomads keep getting absolute bangers. Though, I question who decided to mount the gun under the Chain rifle and not the other way around. Nomad engineers are weird like that.

Another September arrival, the fearsome Tarkshyas is (currently, at least) one of the real powerhouses behind OSS. As you'd expect for a unit with Transmutation, it comes with a separate Operator model.

  • Musterkrux: CB, why do you only release such an awesome model, for such a great profile only after you announce a pending balance pass for Flyers? Such cruelty. I think there may have been an opportunity in designing the visuals of this two-element flyer (Pilot and vehicle) to depart a little from the 'person piloting a machine' aesthetic and CB missed it. Imagine how cool it would be to have the pilot-remote strapped to the under-side like a missile. I mean, why does the robot need a pilot seat and controls if they plug into each other like Voltron? 'I'll form the head' but for a Flyer?
  • Genghis: I have seldom been so conflicted; rules-wise I think the (current) Tarkshya is an abomination which fills me with bitterness, envy and hate. But it looks really cool. Seething.
  • Musterkrux: Seethe and Mald, old man. Go enjoy your collection of amazing Nomad TAGs or something. :)

One of the most hotly anticipated concepts previewed earlier this year is Ioann Bann, a mercenary who will be available to a few factions. Now despite being available for September pre-orders, we have not yet seen any profile for this fine fellow. As a dog warrior type with Transmutation, we expect him to be at least 3VITA, and like long-term dog person McMurrough, we expect him to be a holy terror on the battlefield. One to watch out for in Infinity Army updates.

  • Genghis: Werewolves aren't my favourite part of the Infinity aesthetic, although I really like his body armour. The katanas caused him to be unkindly, but funnily, described as a 'werewolf mall ninja'. We'll see if he walks the walk - I'm probably more interested in the rules than the model.
  • Musterkrux: A werewolf dual-wielding katanas is the perfect combination of cringe, Edge Lord and leftover D&D character templates that I am 100% here for. I will be very interested to see how he differentiates himself from McMurrough.

As the ITS Exclusive sculpt for the next season of ITS, we have Armand Le Muet. Who is a fantastic piece on the table in a game that is slowly circling back to allowing hard AROs to exist once again (Nature is healing). There may be a general release version, so people who desperately need him can either try their luck at winning an event, buying an ITS pack for themselves or just waiting.

  • Musterkrux: That's definitely a model of Armand Le Muet.
  • Genghis: ha, it is fairly straightforward, but it's an impactful unit which I think has been OOP for some time. Pretty decent sniper pose. If I win one I might swap out the head and make it a general-use proxy sniper.

Then there's also Tao Wu, who despite having a fairly modern sculpt gets another one.

  • Musterkrux: I've never really been one for Tao Wu as a character, I don't think CB has ever quite gotten his execution right when it comes to putting a 'mastermind and schemer' on the table. That said, I'm willing to give it another go. Just look at his majestic mustache.
  • Genghis: I guess if I end up with one of these, I can always use the other version as an HVT.

New Book: Hyperthermal

For those who aren't familiar with CB's rules model, this book will not itself contain any new rules. Typically it will release alongside some new units, but even that is not an exact 'release day' thing, the main associated drop of new rules might have been the recent Mazebreaker update, or it might be the Spec-Ops models (see below). But all Infinity rules are free via PDF downloads or the Infinity Army app. The paper books are purely for art and fluff.

What we do know about that fluff is that the book will provide detail on Corregidor, OSS, and Haqqislam.

  • Genghis: I'm often in two minds about the books. The artwork is always gorgeous, and I do find Infinity's universe to be conceptually interesting. However I'm quite critical of how CB have written their narrative in the last few. They tended towards quite dry catalogues of military campaigns, which on fictional planets can blur into a tedious melange. That said there are often little flashes of wit or evocative fiction.

New Spec-Ops Models

The Hyperthermal book (see above) will outline the context or circumstances that warrant the deployment of Spec-Ops across all of the Infinity factions. There may or may not be a McGuffin involved. (There's always a McGuffin)

It looks like each Spec Ops set will contain three models from your chosen faction: The Spec-Ops as Light Infantry, a Heavy Infantry variant, and then an S1 Support Remote buddy.

  • Musterkrux: CB has me dialled in perfectly. I know the whole 'Model Doggo' meme has gone full circle and is a little cringe now but I remain an unashamed Good Boi Enjoyer. I've only had Men Tong for a day and a half and if anything ever happened to him I'd put my opponent into Loss of Lieutenant and then myself.
  • Genghis: I too am willing to be pandered to with regards to miniature pets. I'm reminded of the critical debate around the recent film adaptation of the Odyssey - fundamentally, people have been suckers for a dog for thousands of years.
  • Musterkrux: Look at this guy. He's having a fantastic time. Though, that cod-piece is absolutely medieval. Suspiciously so, though.
  • Genghis: something about the Yu Jing spec ops (pictures of a LI version and a concept art dossier are available online, we haven't included everything) just makes me think he's a huge d-bag. Something about the shades and the jauntily-angled cigar.
  • Musterkrux: My body is ready for the return of Spec-Ops. My read is that they're going to return to the classic box contents where a Spec-Ops comes with multiple weapon options, which is an absolute dream for people who want to weapon-swap other models in their faction. I'm not even sure who is my favorite sculpt there, on one hand I adore Big-Hair PanO but that cheeky grin and sunglasses on the Gui Feng is giving me strong Aura Farming vibes. Overall, I am very excited to see Spec-Ops get more support, the modelling opportunities are massive and communicating the RPG-like progression of a character from their LI incarnation to their Heavy Infantry load-out just sings to me. Bravo, CB.
  • Genghis: god I would love a little sprue of weapons like the old Spec Ops blisters came with. Within the game, though, it's very difficult for them to balance all weapon profiles on units if they're allowed to freely mix-and-match though. I would be fine with a selection of bespoke profiles, like a paramedic with SMG and some utility kit, a plain Specialist Operative with an SWC gun, that sort of thing.

We're also expecting a Combined Army version (Nexus Spec Ops), which was also previewed with LI/HI versions and Remote buddies:

  • Musterkrux: What a happy guy, just living his best life flaying the skin from the upstart sapiens of the Human Sphere.

Additionally, those of you with the wallet-power to pre-order the Hyperthermal book as well as a Spec Ops set will score the Rumbler NA2 Spec Ops. If the Rumbler is the NA2 Spec-Ops, there's no indication whether it comes as a LI/HI pairing or not (or if it gets a Buddy-bot).

  • Musterkrux: I, for one, believe in Cyberpunk Cowboy Batman. You can't just start by perching on gargoyles, you gotta start at the bottom and work your way up, doing all of your brooding on a...Keg of Beer?
  • Genghis: yeah I'm a bit mystified by that as well. Seems like a detail I'd totally lean into for Necromunda (I have some kegs of victory beers as one of my Gang Relic markers) but is out of place for Infinity's futuristic black ops. I might file the letters off and leave it as a generic sci-fi doohickey.

Conclusion

Beyond the immediate releases over the next couple of months (release the Ioann Bann rules now, CB!) this seminar mainly whets our appetite for Hyperthermal and associated releases, notably Spec Ops. We are also keen to see Vehicle re-balancing. There's no surety yet on when that will be, although at an educated guess, we expect something towards the end of this year.

  • Musterkrux: I believe they mentioned it previously that it had encountered some difficulties in securing a production partner but I just want it on the record that I am still deadly keen on that movie/TV-series they previewed a year or two ago. I haven't forgotten, CB.
  • Genghis: Ooh, well remembered. Personally I really want to see the Nomad Spec-Ops models now. I love that they went with HI variants as a standard inclusion. There are a lot of releases in that Spec Ops category though - Infinity has 9 full factions, plus Tohaa (OOP and I wouldn't expect anything) and NA2 (presumably just getting the single Rumbler, not a full set). That is 6 more Spec Ops packs beyond what we've seen previewed here.

Look forward to more coverage from us as and when we get further Infinity news. Tabletop Battles is also looking to expand its WarCrow coverage in the future. If you're interested in that, or in coverage of their upcoming Hexadome Tactics game, please let us know in the comments or by getting in touch directly.

title: Zamanora: Ballad of the Witch Brings Slavic & Balkan Folklore to Life in a New Fantasy TTRPG Setting
content:
Eren Chronicles has launched Zamanora: Ballad of the Witch, a new tabletop role-playing game setting inspired by Slavic and Balkan folklore, on Kickstarter. The campaign, which went live on Tuesday, has already surpassed $120,000 in funding within its first day, making it one of the most notable Dungeons & Dragons 5e campaigns of the year.

Zamanora transports players and Dungeon Masters into a world of rural communities, dark forests, and vengeful witches. The setting is designed to support both Wizards of the Coast’s Dungeons & Dragons 5e and 2024 editions, as well as Legend In The Mist, the rustic fantasy RPG from Son of Oak Game Studio that was recently voted the Most Anticipated TTRPG of 2025.

The Zamanora setting draws heavily from Slavic and Balkan folklore, offering players a chance to explore a world where cautionary tales come to life. Players can create characters from fantastical local creatures such as the mischievous Chorts and the spectral Huants. The setting also introduces unique subclasses, including the Bogatyr fighter, Guslar bard, and Hearth-domain cleric, allowing for thematic storytelling deeply tied to the region’s traditions.

Two new magic systems are introduced in Zamanora: Poppet Magic, a manipulative form of spellcasting, and Ceremonial Magic, which enables non-casters to perform magical rituals. These systems provide fresh ways for players to engage with the game world.

The setting features a variety of mythical creatures familiar to fans of Slavic and Balkan folklore, such as the leshy, baba yaga, and kikimora. These beings are joined by a host of other monsters, each accompanied by detailed descriptions and lore.

The Zamanora Kickstarter offers a range of rewards for backers, from digital PDFs to deluxe collector’s editions. Pledge tiers include options for digital content, physical books, and various accessories. The Core, Deluxe, and Collector’s Boxes include items such as dice, a GMless adventure deck, Baba Yaga miniatures, a DM screen, a monster deck, an illustrated slipcase, and a hand-knitted plushie.

A free demo of the Zamanora setting is available for download on the Kickstarter page, allowing potential backers to explore the world before committing to a pledge.

For more information or to support the project, visit the Zamanora: Ballad of the Witch Kickstarter page.

title: Mantic Games Teases New Fantasy Wargame: Kings of War: Champions

title: New Reinforcements Arrive in Infinity: PanOceania, Yu Jing, Shindenbutai, and Nomads Expand Their Forces
content:
Corvus Belli has introduced a series of new units and expansion packs for its tabletop game, Infinity, bringing additional options to the PanOceania, Yu Jing, and Shindenbutai factions, while also adding the Nomads to the mix.

Kestrel Expansion Pack Beta: PanOceania’s Colonial Forces

The Kestrel Colonial Force is featured in this expansion, showcasing PanOceania’s adaptability in addressing the challenges of space colonization. As a leading power in the Human Sphere, PanOceania leverages its resources to maintain its position, and the Kestrel forces exemplify this approach. Equipped with advanced technology, these units are designed to uphold PanOceania’s strategic interests.

White Banner Expansion Pack Beta: Yu Jing’s Strategic Elite

Yu Jing, often regarded as one of the top powers in the Human Sphere, continues to strengthen its military capabilities with the White Banner Army. This force has demonstrated its effectiveness in conflicts such as the struggle over Svalarheima. Combining cultural heritage with modern technology, the White Banner Army represents Yu Jing’s commitment to achieving its goals through disciplined and strategic action.

Shindenbutai Expansion Pack Beta: Tradition Meets Innovation

On the distant planet of Shinju, the Shindenbutai serve as the military arm of Greater Independent Japan. This force blends traditional samurai values with advanced technology, creating a unique and versatile unit. Tasked with protecting Japanese interests in Shinju’s challenging environment, the Shindenbutai offer players a distinctive option for their armies.

Yu Jing Action Pack and PanOceania Support Pack

The Yu Jing Action Pack provides players with additional units to enhance their armies, reflecting the faction’s combination of cultural depth and technological advancement. Meanwhile, the PanOceania Support Pack introduces specialized units such as the Trauma-Docs and Machinists, which focus on medical support and technical maintenance to keep PanOceanian forces operational.

JSA Support Pack: The Auxiliary Regiment

The Japanese Secessionist Army (JSA) gains new support options with the Tokusetsu Butai, or Auxiliary Regiment. This unit provides essential medical and technical services, ensuring that the JSA’s front-line forces remain effective. The pack highlights the JSA’s emphasis on a balanced approach to warfare, where support units play a critical role.

Nomads Action Pack: A Faction of Free Spirits

The Nomads, known for their independent and unconventional nature, join the battlefield with their own Action Pack. Originating from three massive spaceships that travel the Human Sphere, the Nomads challenge established norms and offer a unique playstyle. Their focus on creativity and adaptability makes them an appealing choice for players seeking a different approach to the game.

title: The Throne of Thorns II for Ruins of Symbaroum 5E Announced: A Darker, More Epic Chapter Awaits
content:
Free League Publishing has announced The Throne of Thorns II, the latest addition to the Ruins of Symbaroum 5th Edition-compatible game line. This new installment continues the epic six-part campaign set in the world of Symbaroum, with pre-orders now available on Free League’s webshop. Those who pre-order will gain access to an alpha-PDF shortly after purchase via DriveThruRPG.

Scheduled for release in June 2025, The Throne of Thorns II is a 230+ page hardcover book that adapts the third and fourth episodes of the Throne of Thorns chronicle for the 5E ruleset. The campaign is designed for characters of 10th to 14th level and is set against a backdrop of escalating tension and danger. The capital city of Yndaros is in chaos as preparations for a royal wedding unfold, while deadly conspiracies threaten to plunge the Davokar region into war. At the same time, a critical wilderness expedition promises to reshape Ambrian history.

The book includes two full-length adventures, The Darkest Star and Mother of Darkness, which form the mid-section and turning point of the Throne of Thorns campaign. It features nearly 20 color maps detailing various locations, such as towns, forests, and ruins, as well as over 60 stat blocks for non-player characters, including monsters, allies, adversaries, and notable individuals. Additionally, the book provides a collection of handouts to enhance gameplay, offering important information for social challenges and problem-solving.

The Throne of Thorns II requires access to the Ruins of Symbaroum Core Setting books—Player’s Guide, Game Master’s Guide, and Bestiary—to fully utilize its content. Fans of the series can now pre-order the book and gain early access to the alpha-PDF, allowing them to prepare for the adventures ahead of the official release.

title: Vesta Mandate: A Competitive Political Thriller TTRPG Launches on Kickstarter
content:
Storygames Chicago has launched Vesta Mandate, a hard sci-fi political intrigue tabletop roleplaying game, on Kickstarter. The campaign will conclude on March 22, offering backers the opportunity to secure the game in either digital or premium hardcover formats.

Set on Vesta Station, a critical hub between Earth and the Outer Rim of the solar system, Vesta Mandate immerses players in a tense political landscape. A century ago, revolutionaries overthrew the Corporation’s control of the station, but now the Vesta Accords are expiring, and the Corporation is returning with threats of force. As members of the Station’s interim government, players take on the roles of ambitious politicians, each with their own vision for the future. Through scheming, negotiation, and betrayal, they must navigate a web of alliances, secrets, and crises to shape the fate of the colony.

Vesta Mandate is a Powered by the Apocalypse (PbtA) storygame enhanced with mechanics and procedures that introduce competitive elements, transforming it into a political drama. Drawing inspiration from games like Pasión de las Pasiones, Carved from Brindlewood, Blades in the Dark, and The Last Caravan, as well as media such as The Expanse, Andor, Silo, and A Memory Called Empire, the game delivers a compelling mix of hard sci-fi and political intrigue.

Designed for 3-5 players, Vesta Mandate can be played as a one-shot or a long-term campaign. Players assume the roles of cunning politicians, each with a Hidden Agenda—a secret plan that evolves into a large-scale coup or power grab. Balancing cooperation and betrayal, players must navigate Secrets, Bonds, and Schisms while responding to escalating crises that threaten the station’s survival.

The game introduces several innovative mechanics to enhance its political drama. Hidden Agendas allow players to co-create secret schemes with the GM, which grow into game-changing power plays. Each character has a scandalous past, known as Secrets, created by other players, which can be used as blackmail. Relationships are central to the game, with Bonds representing alliances and Schisms reflecting conflicts that can escalate into full-blown disputes.

The game uses PbtA-style Moves to resolve tense moments. Players roll two six-sided dice (2d6) and add bonuses based on narrative questions, a mechanic inspired by Pasión de las Pasiones. High-stakes Machinations allow players to burn Bonds for dramatic, game-altering effects.

The game includes five ready-to-run modules, known as Crises, such as Neural Poisoning, Corporate Espionage, and Water Riots. These modules are designed for minimal GM preparation and can be played individually or as part of a larger campaign. Additional Crises are planned as stretch goals.

Backers can choose from a variety of reward tiers, starting at $7 for a digital PDF of the game. Higher tiers include a premium hardcover zine, illustrated by Tony Tran, and a discounted bundle with City of Blood and Plaster, Storygames Chicago’s previous ZineQuest project set in Gilded Age Chicago.

title: Factions Core Rulebook Now Available for Pre-Order
content:
Modiphius Entertainment has announced the pre-order availability of the Fallout: Factions Core Ruleboo. This new hardback rulebook aims to enhance the Fallout: Factions miniature skirmish game, offering players the tools to create campaigns set anywhere in the post-apocalyptic Wasteland.

The Core Rulebook builds on the foundation laid by the Battle for Nuka-World starter set, which featured three raider gangs from Fallout 4’s popular DLC. The new book expands the game’s scope by introducing four additional factions: the Brotherhood of Steel, super mutants, survivors, and raiders. The 112-page, full-color hardcover provides comprehensive rules, campaign systems, and faction-specific content to deepen the gameplay experience.

Priced at £30 / $37, the Core Rulebook will be available for purchase through the Modiphius webstore and local gaming stores in early summer 2025. It is designed to work alongside the Battle for Nuka-World starter set or the upcoming Tokens and Terrain Pack 1, offering players a complete toolkit for creating their own stories in the Wasteland.

The Core Rulebook includes an introduction to wargaming, core rules for fast-paced skirmish gameplay, and an in-depth scenario system to keep each game unique. The Story Phase section allows players to develop their crew, achieve legendary status, or face the consequences of failure. Faction lists provide detailed profiles for each group, including weapons, perks, and legendary characters.

One of the key features of the new rulebook is its flexibility. While the Battle for Nuka-World starter set focused on a specific area, the Core Rulebook allows players to set their campaigns anywhere in the Wasteland. New mechanics, such as Hazards and Facilities, enable crews to customize their Home Turfs, while Objectives and Hazards replace specific scenarios, creating countless combinations for varied gameplay.

Players can also hire new Legends of the Wasteland, upgrade weapons, purchase chems, and unlock perks for their crew. The updated Story Phase ensures campaigns are more expansive and interconnected, offering greater opportunities for storytelling and strategic decision-making.

title: Wrath of the Wyvern: A Dark Fantasy Solo TTRPG Launches on Kickstarter
content:
A new dark fantasy solo tabletop role-playing game, Wrath of the Wyvern, has launched on Kickstarter. Set in the Umbral Highlands, a land where humanity struggles to survive under the threat of monstrous wyverns, the game casts players as a lone hunter tasked with reclaiming the world from these fearsome creatures. Inspired by Scottish Celtic mythology, the game blends exploration, survival, and tactical combat into a solo RPG experience.

Wrath of the Wyvern introduces a Fate Card system, which replaces traditional dice rolls. This system, powered by the Fury Engine, is designed to create fast-paced, strategic, and cinematic encounters. Players navigate an open-world hexcrawl, making decisions that influence the fate of the Highlands. The game emphasizes replayability, with branching storylines and faction dynamics adding depth to each playthrough.

Combat is a central element, utilizing a custom Tarot-sized card deck to manage attacks, defenses, and special abilities. Players spend Stamina Points (SP) to execute actions and must adapt to the unique behaviors of their enemies. Survival mechanics, such as hunger, exhaustion, and changing weather conditions, further enhance the exploration experience.

The Umbral Highlands are a perilous and richly detailed world. Players will encounter legendary monsters from Scottish folklore, including the Wulver, Ghillie Dhu, and Kelpie, as well as the game’s primary antagonists: the Sons of Rivesk, ancient and formidable wyverns. Each wyvern battle is a multi-phase event, requiring careful planning and strategy.

In addition to hunting wyverns, players can rebuild Crag Keep, the ruined fortress of the Skyfire Order, and recruit allies to aid in their quest. The game also features arcane powers and legendary weapons, offering players opportunities to wield powerful magic and craft unique tools.

Backers of Wrath of the Wyvern will receive a premium package that includes a 140+ page hardcover rulebook, a massive hexcrawl map of the Umbral Highlands, a Wyvern Showdown battlemap, a hero miniature, and access to the Isle of Skye expansion. The game will be available in English, Spanish, Italian, and French, with each translation handled by a native speaker.

The campaign will run until April 3, giving potential backers 28 days to pledge their support.

title: This Monty Python-esque comedy RPG lets you improv as a band of incompetent and dangerously powerful wizards
content:
Hello Wizard I Have a Problem is a new tabletop roleplaying game that allows players to become powerful and incompetent spellcasters.

The upcoming roleplaying game sees any number of players collaborating together to tell a story about a band of chaotic wizards. Similarly to the likes of absurdist, fantastical comedy such as the works of iconic British group Monty Python, alongside the likes of The Mighty Boosh and What We Do in the Shadows, Hello Wizard I have a Problem is all about rapid scenes infused by the strange and unexpected.

Unlike many other tabletop RPGs, Hello Wizard sees its players taking turns to take on the roles of player character and games master. Each scene in Hello Wizard has a single player take the spotlight as their spellcaster, with the goal of impressing their fellow sorcerers with their magic. The active player describes what spells their wizard casts, with the other players acting collectively as a GM and deciding how these spells can go wrong.

Players will use a Problem Generator included in the fantasy RPG’s rulebook as inspiration for what could go wrong with the wizards’ spells, with the book capable of making over “200,000” prompts for possible disastrous outcomes. Once every player has had the opportunity to step into the spellcasting spotlight at least a few times, the game ends and players tally up their ‘points’ - which are decided by a loose improv system - and determine who is the most impressive wizard.

The rules system for Hello Wizard is very straightforward and intended to be easy for players to learn. Setup for the tabletop RPG is also designed to be quick and easy, with players expected to start in little time. The rulebook for the game will contain advice and optional rules players can use to augment their playthroughs too.

Hello Wizard I have a Problem was created by Sam Armstrong, a tabletop RPG designer who has previously made titles such as All Bastard - a fantasy TRPG in which players take the roles of either a band of bragging heroes or the bastards they defeated - and horror roleplaying game Slasher. The artwork for the game was created by illustrator Evlyn Moreau, who has previously worked on RPGs like Liminal High School.

The crowdfunding campaign for Hello Wizard I Have a Problem is on Kickstarter until later this afternoon, with the title potentially being made available on Armstrong’s Itch.io page. A pledge of £8 ($10) will get backers a physical copy of the game in June, alternatively a PDF version is available for £4 ($5).

title: Re-enact Greta Gerwig’s Little Women with this coming-of-age tabletop RPG
content:
New tabletop roleplaying game, Castles in the Air, will enable players to re-enact their favourite coming-of-age stories.

Castles in the Air was inspired by the likes of classic coming-of-age period dramas such as Little Women by Louisa May Alcott - which was adapted into a 2019 film directed by Greta Gerwig and starring Saoirse Ronan, Emma Watson, Florence Pugh, Laura Dern and Timothee Chalamet - and Anne of Green Gables by Lucy Maud Montgomery, which was adapted into a televisions series in 2017 by Netflix.

The upcoming roleplaying game will see players’ characters grow up together from children to adults during the historical era known as the Gilded Age, which took place in the USA from the 1870s to the 1890s and saw an increase in industrialisation, economic growth and migration to the US. Castles in the Air is a collaborative storytelling game in which players construct narratives that centre around the wonders and fears of childhood, before tackling the joys and hardships of adulthood.

Players begin the tabletop RPG as a tight-knit group of children, all of whom have great expectations of their futures and much quieter current lives. In this phase of the story, players develop a shared childhood together by doing the things rural and financially supported kids did during that era: like playing in their local farmlands, swimming in the lakes and watching the stars.

As the player characters grow up, they’ll begin exploring other feelings and ideas that come with age. Characters in the group might develop a crush on someone or form a heated rivalry with one of the other local children. All the while, the player group will grow up together, before eventually reaching adulthood and potentially finding themselves drifting apart as life takes them in different directions - perhaps to only meet once again.

Players will be able to create their characters in Castles in the Air by choosing from a variety of character roles inspired by classic archetypes, such as the troublesome scamp, studious bookworm or spoiled princess. Add onto this a dream, childhood relationships, a family background and a bosom enemy, and players can even create their favourite characters from the likes of Little Women or Anne of Green Gables.

Castles in the Air was designed and written by Melia Carraway, with contributions from co-created by the co-founders of the RPG’s publisher, Storybrewer’s Roleplaying, Vee Hendro and Hayley Gordon, who also co-designed Good Society: a tabletop RPG inspired by the works of Jane Austen.

The crowdfunding campaign for Castles in the Air is on Kickstarter until June 9th, with a pledge of AU$ 99 (£52/$77) getting backers a physical copy of the game in March 2025. Alternatively, players can get a digital version for a pledge of AU$ 34 (£18/$26).

title: Freak War throws Exploding Kittens and Pokémon into a blender for a trading card game you can play at parties
content:
Take the evolving monsters of Pokémon, cross them with the fast-playing chaos of party game hit Exploding Kittens and you end up with something that looks a lot like Freak War, a new party-game TCG that wants to offer the fun battles of trading card games without the effort of learning lots of rules or building a deck.

Freak War is the creation of Nate Galbraith, aka cartoonist sketchnate, who was inspired after watching kids trying to have Pokémon battles using Uno cards, before suggesting they play classic playing card game War (which you might also know as Battle) instead. The result was a mixture of all three, with Galbraith adding a collection of strange creatures to the cards.

Unlike the head-to-head battles of Pokémon, Freak War can be played with up to four (or more) players, who can simply split the shuffled deck between them to play - though there is the option to build your own custom decks if you really want to.

Everyone plays a creature at the same time, with the highest attack level winning the battle. Like Exploding Kittens, the many cards can also introduce various effects that shake things up, including the power to evolve into bigger creatures - Pokémon-style - and equip modifiers to your own or opponent’s cards to boost or reduce their strength.

Whether the players choose a card from their hand or simply flip the top of their deck depends on the mode they’re playing: the more chaotic War, or the more strategic Battle. Both modes can be modified further by King of the Hill and team rules.

If two players draw in attack level, they both discard a card before facing off by playing another creature. The overall winner takes all the cards played and adds them to their win pile, which are reshuffled into the player’s deck - the person who manages to claim all the cards from their opponents, wins.

The weird and wonderful creatures on the cards have a bit of lore behind them, having been created by the emergence of a second sun that mutated familiar animals like rabbits, foxes and fish into muscly fishpeople, a time-travelling tiger, a partying platypus, a dog with a goldfish bowl for a head, a sad bee and a Man Cat that appears to basically be a bloke in a cat costume, among others.

Modifier cards, meanwhile, range from a Super Sword (and a Super Duper Sword) to the power to swap cards with a rival, cancel a modifier or flip coins for the chance of a power boost. Some of the creature effects get playfully meta in the way you’d expect for a party game too, with the scrap-loving Fly Guy gaining power if there’s uneaten food near the players.

As someone who is admittedly tired of many copy-paste or just downright gross party games (looking at you, double-offending Cards Against Humanity clones), I’m fairly charmed by Galbraith’s goofy creations and the sprinkling of chaotic take-that gameplay in the form of a TCG. (The card layout is quite explicitly inspired by Pokémon cards.) Sure, it’s not going to be for everyone, but as something knowingly silly to fill five minutes with friends and family (especially younger players), it looks like solid, breezy fun for $20 a deck. With a bunch of different packs filled with dozens more creatures from buff penguins to cute-looking snails, I’m pretty intrigued just to see Galbraith’s interpretation of the nonsense of modern Pokémon evolutions, too.

Freak War has already passed its fairly modest crowdfunding goal of $10,000 over on Kickstarter, where its campaign will run until June 13th. The game itself is expected to land with backers next June, just in time to take on holiday.

title: New Blade Runner RPG expansion asks how far you’d go for the Replicant Rebellion
content:
A new expansion for the official Blade Runner tabletop roleplaying game invites you to join the Replicant Rebellion.

Blade Runner: The Roleplaying Game is based on the series of films based on Phillip K Dick’s sci-fi novel Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep.

Blade Runner, the first of these films, was released in 1982 and directed by Ridley Scott. The film sees Harrison Ford play Deckard, a Blade Runner - an officer whose sole purpose is to hunt and eliminate Replicants, or human-looking androids - who is tasked with finding and killing three escaped Replicants. Following on from the original film, Blade Runner 2049 is a sequel directed by Denis Villeneuve and starring Ryan Gosling. In Blade Runner 2049, Gosling stars as K, a Replicant Blade Runner who must follow the trail of a long-escaped Replicant fugitive and investigate the truth behind her death.

Both films take place in the same fictional science fiction universe wherein Replicants were designed and created entirely to fulfil the needs and wants of their human makers. The Blade Runner franchise is known for its cyberpunk aesthetics, as well as grim view of a near-future wherein corporations are able to commit terrible acts without consequence and exploit large swathes of people.

Blade Runner: The Roleplaying Game usually has players taking the roles of Blade Runners within the LA police department during the time period between the first and second films. However, rather than fulfilling their duties as Replicant hunting officers, the next expansion for the sci-fi RPG sees players abandoning their post to join the Replicant Underground.

Replicant Rebellion is a new expansion for the Blade Runner RPG that sees players get recruited into the Replicant Underground, a secret organisation whose goal is to ensure the freedom and liberation of Replicants: whatever the cost.

Players will see themselves become members of the movement - running their own independent crew as they carry out a variety of missions on behalf of the Underground. From laying charges for explosives, sabotaging the Replicant trade and smoking out moles, players must be prepared for all manner of tasks. Members of the group might even find themselves stuck between a rock and a hard place, as they balance their personal morality with the operations of the Replicant Underground.

Both the Replicant Rebellion expansion and the Blade Runner roleplaying game were published and created by Free League Publishing, the studio behind other licensed TRPGs such as the Alien Roleplaying Game.

A crowdfunding campaign for Blade Runner: The Roleplaying Game - Replicant Rebellion will be launched on Kickstarter on May 28th.

title: City of Six Moons is a board game written in an alien language you’ll need to translate to play - and you’ll never know if you’ve got it quite right
content:
Upcoming board game City of Six Moons is taking difficulty-to-decipher rulebooks to a whole new level by writing all of its rules in an alien language that you’ll have to translate in order to play. The kicker? You’ll never know if you’ve done so correctly.

The single-player title is described by designer Amabel Holland as being both a game about guiding the fortunes of an alien civilisation, and a game designed as if it actually were made by an alien civilisation in real life.

As such, Holland has written the entire rulebook in a language composed of icons, glyphs and symbols, setting a challenge to the player to decipher the language before they can read the rules for the game itself. To work out its secrets, you’ll apparently need to draw on both your own existing cultural assumptions and the acceptance that the culture of the alien civilisation who made it is very different to humanity.

Cheekily, Holland proposes that players will never quite know if they’ve perfectly cracked the code, and she will refuse to answer any questions about the game’s rules. (Well spotted, BoardGameGeek.)

Given all that, we obviously don’t quite know how the game will play, or even how long it'll take to finish, only that it’ll be a solitaire experience with a set of components needed to play the game in the box alongside the rulebook. Presumably those components will either be devoid of language or marked in the same code as the rules, though we also don’t know what game pieces will be included just yet. We have seen the cover artwork at least, which presumably might offer a first clue to decoding the iconographic language.

Holland did confirm over on Bluesky that City of Six Moons will be a “functional, replayable game” for those who do successfully figure out its rules (or enough to play, that is), though deciphering the code is considered a key part of the package - meaning that players might find it a “lesser” experience after they know its secrets. Yet even that permanent change in understanding is part of the overall journey, Holland believes: “That loss is a thing I want you to feel; I want it to linger.”

City of Six Moons is due for release next month from Holland’s own (alongside co-owner Mary Holland) publishing label Hollandspiele. Good luck to anyone preparing to tackle the cryptic puzzle.

title: Alternate cover for Dungeons & Dragons’ Player’s Handbook radiates a wholesome vibe for players who want to D&D and chill
content:
The front cover for the alternate version of the next Dungeons & Dragons Player Handbook has been revealed.

Last week saw the unveiling of the artwork for the front cover of the Player’s Handbook, for the next version of tabletop roleplaying game - Dungeons & Dragons. Featuring depictions of classic characters from the history of the RPG - such as Strongheart the Knight, Elkhorn the Dwarf Warrior and Yolande the Elven Queen - the front cover shows a party of D&D adventurers and heroes preparing to fight against a horde of Kobolds, a classic Dungeons & Dragons enemy, with a friendly golden dragon standing behind them.

The artwork strongly implies that the group is in the midst of a battle, thereby emphasising the action elements of the fantasy roleplaying game over anything else - which is what D&D is largely known for, at least amongst the general public.

By contrast, the artwork for the front cover of the alternate version of the new D&D Player’s Handbook was revealed soon afterwards - showing a much different approach. (Thanks Polygon) Designed for collectors or players who aren’t keen on the appearance of the standard version, the alternative versions of D&D books don’t differ much from their standard counterparts beyond the outside aesthetics and front cover.

The artwork for the cover of the alternate version of the next D&D Player’s Handbook also depicts a party of adventurers, this time in a very different situation from those shown on the front of the standard book. A classic Dungeons & Dragons party - complete with wizard, cleric, fighter and rogue - are shown sharing a pot of tea inside what looks like the inside of a cave. Included within this serene tea party is a golden dragon - somewhat linking things back to the standard cover - who grasps a normal-sized tea cup in one massive paw, with the party’s rogue balancing on part of the dragon’s body above.

This illustration by artist Wylie Beckert, who is also responsible for the front cover of the alternative version of Dungeon & Dragons: Tasha’s Cauldron of Everything, certainly gives off a very different vibe to that of the cover for the standard version of the new Player’s Handbook, which was created by Tyler Jacobsen, providing players who prefer a more relaxed and introspective approach to roleplaying with a more suitable option.

The alternate version of the new D&D Player’s Handbook will be available from local game stores from September 3rd, before the wider release of the book on September 17th.
